outcome: No proof or disproof of infinitude, and no new base-2 Cullen prime, has appeared since 26 January 2024; the largest known Cullen prime remains 6679881·2^6679881+1, found in 2009.
summary: The question is whether there are infinitely many Cullen primes (numbers of the form n·2^n+1 that are prime). The current Wikipedia article on Cullen numbers, t5k.org's (Prime Pages) list of the largest known Cullen primes, and its top-20 Cullen primes page all still show exactly sixteen known Cullen primes, with the largest being 6679881·2^6679881+1, discovered in 2009 — no new base-2 Cullen prime has been found since the frozen revision, and no proof or disproof of infinitude has appeared. The one piece of related activity found in this window is PrimeGrid's Generalized Cullen Prime Search, which in April 2025 found a new largest generalized Cullen prime, 4052186·69^4052186+1 (base 69) — but generalized Cullen numbers (n·b^n+1 for general base b) are a distinct, broader family from the base-2 Cullen numbers this problem concerns, and per §3.1 a different base is a related/variant problem, not a case of this one (settling it removes no territory from the base-2 question). Even setting that scope issue aside, per §3.1 an infinitude question is not advanced by a new example or an extended search bound in any case — only an actual proof or disproof would move it, and none exists. As an aside, Hooley's 1976 result that almost all Cullen numbers are composite, and Caldwell's conjecture that infinitely many are nonetheless prime, both predate the window and are unchanged. No AI involvement was found anywhere in this space; the generalized Cullen search is conducted by PrimeGrid's traditional distributed sieving/PRP (Proth-type) testing infrastructure, not any AI/ML system. This is a well-evidenced 'nothing happened' record.
competing_reading: One could argue the base-69 generalized Cullen prime result is worth noting as adjacent activity in the same research community (PrimeGrid) that also runs the (currently apparently inactive) base-2 Cullen search, suggesting the general topic is not dormant even though the base-2 problem itself hasn't moved. But this doesn't change the classification: it is a different base, hence a different (related) problem under §3.1, and even a genuine base-2 discovery would not resolve an infinitude question.
what_would_settle_it: A proof or disproof of infinitude of base-2 Cullen primes, or (short of that) an announcement from PrimeGrid's Cullen Prime Search (base 2 specifically) of a seventeenth known Cullen prime, which would still leave the infinitude question open but would at least update the 'known Cullen primes' record referenced in the article.
